# Shared facet pyramids, exact cap response, and the remaining extremal interface

This note proves an actual compatible deformation and its simultaneous cap response. It also records the precise scope of the archived extremal route. Neither the deformation nor the final proposed overlap inequality is claimed to establish OC.

UPDATE: the arbitrary-body limitation stated for the old flux source in
Section 5 has now been removed by
`candidate 7127f9c7b67df7cb`,
using actual support-plane disintegration and fiber Gauss–Green. That
extension also corrects the integer-coordinate cap-covariance sign.
The numerical overlap inequality remains unproved. The visible-star
first-order tests themselves are already implied by face-preserving
transport, as proved in
`candidate 332fa99ca9bb69c2`.

Throughout Sections 1–4, `d>=1`. Mixed volume is the sum of ordinary `d`-volumes over the finitely many integer bases. The bodies used there are full-dimensional polytopes with positive-volume fibers at every integer base in their projection. This is an explicit restriction of the new facet construction, not an assertion that an unrestricted OC minimum is polyhedral.

## 1. One actual ambient facet and one actual deformation

Let `C` be such a polytope, and let

    F = C intersect {a.z+u.x=b},       |u|=1,

be a nonvertical facet, with `C` on the `<=b` side. Choose `w0=(p0,x0)` in `F` and a continuous displacement `v` such that `u.v=1`. Suppose that, for all sufficiently small positive `epsilon`,

    q_epsilon=w0+epsilon(0,v)

satisfies every other facet inequality of `C`. This condition holds, for example, if `w0` is in the relative interior of `F`. If `w0` is on other facets, the condition is exactly that their outward continuous normals have nonpositive pairing with `v`; the remaining strict inequalities persist for small `epsilon`.

Set

    C_epsilon=conv(C,q_epsilon).

The integer-coordinate projection does not change because `p0` belongs to the projection of `C`. Thus the finite integer base set is unchanged. All fiber inclusions required by ambient convexity hold automatically.

Define the facet roof

    T(w)=max{t in [0,1]: w=t w0+(1-t)f for some f in F}.

The maximum exists by compactness. For `0<=t<1`,

    {w in F:T(w)>=t}=t w0+(1-t)F.                    (1)

In particular, `T` is a nonnegative concave polyhedral function on `F`.

**Pyramid identity.** The added part of `C_epsilon` is, up to its common boundary with `C`, exactly

    {w+s epsilon(0,v): w in F, 0<=s<=T(w)}.          (2)

Proof. The apex violates only the inequality defining `F`. Any segment from the apex to a point of `C` first enters `C` on `F`: all other inequalities hold throughout the segment. Therefore `C_epsilon=C union conv(F,q_epsilon)`. Writing a point of the latter pyramid as `t q_epsilon+(1-t)f` gives (2); the converse follows from the definition of `T` and the nested homothetic sets in (1). The representation in (2) is unique away from parameter boundary identifications: the facet functional gives `s=(a.z+u.x-b)/epsilon`, after which `w` is determined. This also proves that there is no overlapping-volume charge.

Let `P` be the integer base set and write

    eta_F = sum_(z in P) H_(d-1) restricted to F_z.

The normalization `|u|=1` gives unit fiberwise normal Jacobian in (2), regardless of the tangential part of `v`. Consequently the exact, finite-`epsilon` mass identity is

    M(C_epsilon)-M(C) = epsilon A,
    A = integral_F T d eta_F.                        (3)

Here `H_0` is counting measure when `d=1`. A facet section of dimension less than `d-1` contributes zero; a section with `T=0` also contributes zero. These cases are not silently deleted from a positive measure.

Layer cake gives an arithmetic identity retaining the sampled fibers:

    A = sum_(z in P) integral_0^1 (1-t)^(d-1)
          H_(d-1)(F_((z-t p0)/(1-t))) dt.             (4)

The index inside the integral is a real base. Formula (4) is an exact slice of the actual facet at that base, not a replacement of the sum over integer fibers by an integral over the projection. The endpoint `t=1` is irrelevant to the integral, including when `d=1`.

## 2. Every closed ambient cap uses the same added measure

For an ambient affine functional `ell(z,x)`, write `v_ell` for its continuous normal and let `H={ell>=0}`. Then

    lim_(epsilon down to 0)
       [M(C_epsilon intersect H)-M(C intersect H)]/epsilon
       = integral_F T chi_H^+ d eta_F,               (5)

where `chi_H^+(w)` equals one if either `ell(w)>0`, or `ell(w)=0` and `v_ell.v>=0`, and equals zero otherwise.

Indeed, after dividing the exact added-pyramid integral by `epsilon`, the integrand is

    integral_0^T(w) 1_{ell(w)+epsilon s v_ell.v>=0} ds.

Its pointwise limit is `T(w)chi_H^+(w)`, bounded by `T(w)`. Dominated convergence proves (5). Thus oblique normals, positive boundary mass, a tangent outward displacement, and closed-halfspace conventions are all explicit. In the additional case `eta_F({ell=0})=0`, the right side is simply the mass of `H` for the single measure `T eta_F`.

## 3. Exact circuit cover and its regular first response

Consider finitely many caps `H_j={ell_j>=0}` through one actual point `(p,y)` on an integer fiber. Let their continuous normals be `v_j!=0`, and suppose positive numbers `rho_j` satisfy `sum rho_j v_j=0`. Assume every cap has the same mixed mass `Q`. Define

    S_j = sum_z H_(d-1)(C_z intersect {ell_j(z,.)=0})/|v_j|.

For this section assume the threshold-volume functions are differentiable at zero with derivative `-S_j`, with `S_j>0`, and this derivative is continuous in a threshold neighborhood. It suffices that every fiber cut is proper, strictly empty, or strictly full. More generally supporting cuts with null `(d-1)`-measure are allowed if the stated regularity is verified. Also assume `eta_F({ell_j=0})=0`. These hypotheses deliberately exclude an unproved linearization across a positive supporting facet.

For small `epsilon`, choose threshold shifts `s_j(epsilon)` and a common cap mass `tau(epsilon)` by

    M(C_epsilon intersect {ell_j>=s_j})=tau,
    sum_j rho_j s_j=0.                               (6)

They exist uniquely locally. Each cap volume is strictly decreasing in its threshold near zero, so its inverse is continuous. The weighted sum of the inverse thresholds is strictly decreasing in `tau`, changes sign on a sufficiently small interval around `Q`, and hence has a unique zero. Formula (5) and the original threshold derivatives give, uniformly for shifts of order `epsilon`,

    s_j = [epsilon B_j-(tau-Q)]/S_j+o(epsilon+|tau-Q|),
    B_j = integral_F T 1_(H_j) d eta_F.

The inverse equation first bounds `tau-Q=O(epsilon)`, and then gives

    tau'(0+) = sum_j theta_j B_j,
    theta_j = (rho_j/S_j)/(sum_l rho_l/S_l).           (7)

The shifted caps in (6) cover the **whole fiber** at `p`, not just a neighborhood of `y`. Their weighted affine functionals sum to zero on that fiber. Therefore all of them cannot be strictly negative at any point. This exact cover property does not rely on an approximate meeting point or on a rounded center.

With

    W=sum_j theta_j 1_(H_j),        beta=Q/M(C),

the normalized upper-bound derivative is

    tau'(0+)-beta M'(0+)
       = integral_F T(W-beta) d eta_F.               (8)

For several selected circuit groups the **same** measure `T eta_F` occurs in every instance of (8). If their exact covers, together with uniformly slack cap covers on the other fibers, control every mixed point, then all the quantities in (8) being negative implies a strict decrease of the global normalized maximum depth. This is an actual all-source bound: every point is covered by a cap whose reoptimized mass is controlled.

## 4. What can fail, and what this calculation retains

The coefficient `A` can be zero even for a nontrivial ambient pyramid, because the roof may vanish on every sampled facet section. An integer-base apex on a facet boundary can avoid that problem, but then its motion must satisfy the other active facet inequalities. A construction that simply bulges one fiber and ignores those inequalities is not (2).

Positive boundary mass is fully handled in (5), but the reoptimization formula (7) has an explicit regularity restriction. With coincident supporting cuts, one must instead use the archived one-sided allocation/quantile response. Replacing that response by (7) without checking the hypotheses would lose the boundary-mass cases of OC.

Likewise, existence of an unrestricted positive attained minimum does not imply that it has an ambient facet. Sections 1–3 supply a independently testable polytopal mechanism and an exact shared-cap coefficient; they do not supply a polyhedral reduction.

## 5. Exact dependency graph of the general extremal route

The following dependencies are already proved in the cited archive, with the indicated scope.

1. Canonical normalization and attained-minimum compactness preserve the number `k` of occupied parity classes in the positive-volume problem. The relevant target is `Gamma_d/k`, and `k<=2^n`.
2. Fixed deepest-face witnesses reduce the relevant genuine critical covers to at most `k` groups. Each group has a positive projected normal circuit. Other fibers have slack covers. See `candidate 4a38a3cfd6733dce`.
3. Actual convex-potential erosions work for arbitrary convex fibers and preserve ambient compatibility. Their normal velocities, cap one-sided derivatives, and normalized stress separation are proved in `candidate a68c14b477a24d06`. Signed joint homothety fixes the separated stress normalization `sum lambda=1/beta`.
4. Positive supporting-facet mass requires the inside/outside allocation quantifiers in `candidate 9c6d3cb586898f7e`. Every admissible inside allocation has some compensating outside allocation; neither a free choice of both nor a common choice for all unrelated circuits has been proved.
5. The resulting convex-order inequality has an actual physical boundary martingale whose destinations stay on the same ambient support face. This is `candidate 7278f286325c46c7`. The originally polytopal covariance-flux formulas are now extended, with the corrected integer-coordinate sign, by `candidate 7127f9c7b67df7cb`. That extension retains the explicit section-centroid hypotheses and gives no numerical sign bound for the resulting mixed terms.

For a regular chosen cover, write `eta` for the full fiber boundary measure and `W_i=sum_j theta_ij 1_(H_ij)`. An actual nonnegative convex-potential inward velocity `-Phi` has response

    beta integral Phi d eta - integral Phi W_i d eta. (9)

Thus a concrete sufficient new quantitative statement would be that the actual compatible test class contains a `Phi` with

    min_i [integral Phi W_i d eta / integral Phi d eta]
           >= Gamma_d/k,                            (10)

with positive denominator. At a hypothetical minimum with `beta<Gamma_d/k`, (9) would strictly improve every group. This is an explicitly stated common boundary-overlap inequality on the actual geometry. It is **not proved here**. Its nonsmooth extension must retain the allocation quantifiers in item 4. The shared pyramid calculation gives a second, outward, test family with the opposite sign in (8).

The new all-status anchored residual theorem strengthens the premises by adding actual cap-volume inequalities for every anchored convex relation, including full-residual escape and overlap-safe packing. It does not by itself bound the boundary integrals in (10): its coefficients involve volumes, whereas (9) uses a common physical boundary location and section-dependent circuit weights. The exact three-fiber scalar obstruction in `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)` forbids replacing this missing directional information by masses alone. Similarly, the archived midpoint-defect obstruction shows that restricting to integral midpoint charges loses higher-arity anchored relations.

The independently falsifiable local problem is therefore to compare the **one common** measure in (8) or (9) with all actual circuit profiles, subject to the genuine shared-face geometry and anchored residual inclusions. No existence of a paying facet, a paying potential, or a global allocation is asserted by this note.

## 6. A complete visible facet star, including positive mixed seam overlap

The single-facet feasibility restriction can be removed within the polytopal setting. Choose any `w0=(p0,x0)` in `C`, any continuous vector `v`, and put `C_epsilon=conv(C,w0+epsilon(0,v))`. The projection is again unchanged. Normalize each nonvertical facet inequality as

    L_i(z,x)=a_i.z+u_i.x-b_i<=0,       |u_i|=1.

For small positive `epsilon`, the visible facets are exactly

    I_+={i:L_i(w0)=0, c_i=u_i.v>0}.                  (11)

All strictly inactive inequalities remain satisfied; vertical inequalities cannot be violated by this displacement. The new region is the union of the visible pyramids `conv(F_i,w0+epsilon(0,v))`. For each `i`, let `T_i` be its roof defined as in Section 1. Its fiberwise Jacobian is now `epsilon c_i`.

**Overlap lemma.** At a fixed integer base `z`, two distinct visible pyramids have intersection of positive `d`-volume only if

    u_i=u_j and b_i-a_i.z=b_j-a_j.z.                 (12)

When (12) holds, their entire fiber slices coincide, including their roofs.

Proof. If an exterior point lies in both pyramids, the ray from the apex through it has a unique first intersection with `C`. That intersection belongs to `F_i intersect F_j`; a segment toward a visible facet cannot enter `C` before reaching its facet plane. The common pyramid therefore lies in

    c_j L_i-c_i L_j=0.

Its continuous normal is `c_j u_i-c_i u_j`. Unless this is zero, its intersection with a fixed fiber has dimension at most `d-1` and hence zero `d`-volume. If it is zero, the positive `c_i,c_j` and unit normalizations force `u_i=u_j`, hence `c_i=c_j`; a nonempty overlap then forces the support equality in (12).

For the final assertion, both `w0` and a base `z` satisfying (12) lie in the affine zero set of `L_i-L_j`, whose continuous part is zero. At every real base `(z-t p0)/(1-t)`, this difference still vanishes. The two facet slices there are exactly the same subset of `C`. Applying the roof superlevel identity (1) at every `0<=t<1` proves that the two roofs and complete pyramid slices at `z` coincide.

For each `z`, retain one representative from each equivalence class (12), using a fixed ordering of the finitely many facets, and call the resulting set `I_z`. Define a single finite measure on the original fiber boundaries by

    d xi(z,x) = sum_(i in I_z) c_i T_i(z,x)
                      dH_(d-1)|_(F_i)_z.            (13)

Then the exact mass identity and every closed cap derivative are

    M(C_epsilon)-M(C)=epsilon xi(total),
    [M(C_epsilon intersect H)-M(C intersect H)]/epsilon
          -> integral chi_H^+ d xi.                  (14)

The same `chi_H^+` as in (5), using the one actual displacement `v`, applies. The overlap lemma justifies (14) fiber by fiber; it does not discard an ambient-null set that carries positive mixed volume. Under the regularity hypotheses of Section 3, its simultaneous circuit response is exactly

    tau_i'(0+)-beta M'(0+)=integral (W_i-beta) d xi.  (15)

If `p0` is an integer base with a full-dimensional fiber and `v` points strictly outside that fiber at `x0`, then `xi(total)>0`. Indeed, at least one ordinary facet of `C_p0` containing `x0` has positive outward pairing with `v`; its ordinary pyramid already has positive volume proportional to `epsilon` and is contained in the added fiber. Thus the complete star gives a nontrivial actual deformation at any such outward direction, even when no single facet can be moved alone.

Here is the simplest reason the representative rule is indispensable. In `R times R`, let

    C={-1<=z<=1, -1<=x, x+z<=1, x-z<=1},
    w0=(0,1),       v=1.

The two roof facets are both visible. At integer base zero, each visible pyramid adds exactly the same interval `[1,1+epsilon]`; at bases `-1,1` it adds no length. Actual mixed length increases by `epsilon`, whereas an unqualified sum over the two ambient pyramids gives `2 epsilon`. Formula (12) identifies the two coincident slices at zero and (14) gives the correct value. This example has positive original fibers at all three integer bases.

This star construction remains polytopal. In an arbitrary body a small apex addition can have zero first-order volume, so (13) is not silently extended to a curved support point. It supplies a finite actual deformation class and a rigorously shared cap measure, not the unproved uniform quantitative sign in (15).
